s: The story of Moses is one of the most beautiful and fascinating stories in all the world.
It takes hold of us and never for an instant loses its interest, for it is told so vividly that once heard it is never forgotten.
I have often imagined the anxiety with which that child was born, for he came into the world with a sentence of death hanging over him, since Pharaoh had decreed that the male children should die.
The mother defied even the command of the king and determined that the child should live, and right from the beginning the battle of right against might was fought at the cradle.
The mother of Moses was a slave.
She had to work in the brickyards or labor in the fields, but God was on her side and she won, as a mother always wins with God on her side.

Before going to work she had to choose some hiding place for her child, and she put his little sister, Miriam, on guard while she kept herself from being seen by the soldiers of Pharaoh, who were searching everywhere to murder the Jewish male children.
For three months she kept him hidden, possibly finding a new hiding place every few days.
It is hard to imagine anything more difficult than hiding a healthy, growing baby, and he was hidden for three months.
Now he had grown larger and more full of life, and a safer hiding place had to be found, and I can imagine this mother giving up her rest and sleep to prepare an ark for the saving of her child.
I believe the plan must have been formed in heaven.

I have often thought that God must have been as much interested in that work as the mother of Moses was, for you can't make me believe that an event so important as that, and so far-reaching in its results, ever happened by luck or chance.
Possibly God whispered the plan to the mother when she went to Him in prayer and in her grief, because she was afraid the sword of Pharaoh would murder her child.
And how carefully the material from which the ark was made had to be selected!
I think every twig was carefully examined so that nothing poor might get into its makeup, and into the weaving of that ark the mother's heart, her soul, her prayers and her tears were interwoven.

Oh, if you mothers would exercise as much care over the company your children keep, over the books they read and the places they go, there would not be so many girls feeding the red-light district, nor so many boys growing up to lead criminal lives.

And with what thanksgiving she must have poured out her heart when at last the work was done and the ark was ready to carry its precious cargo, more precious than if it were to hold the crown jewels of Egypt.
And I can imagine the last night that baby spent in the home.
Probably some of you can remember when the last night came that your baby was alive; you can remember the last night the coffin stayed, and the next day when the pallbearers and the hearse came.
The others may have slept soundly, but there was no sleep for you, and I can imagine there was no sleep for the mother of Moses.

"There are whips and tops and pieces of string
And shoes that no little feet ever wear;
There are bits of ribbon and broken wings
And locks of golden hair.

"There are dainty jackets that are never worn,
There are toys and models of ships;
There are books and pictures all faded and torn
And marked by the fingertips
Of dimpled hands that have fallen to dust—
Yet we strive to believe that the Lord is just.

"Yet a feeling of bitterness fills our soul;
Sometimes we try to pray,
That the Reaper has spared so many flowers
And taken ours away.
And we sometimes doubt if the Lord can know
How our broken hearts loved them so.

"But we think of our dear ones dead,
Our children who never grow old,
And how they are waiting and watching for us
In the city with streets of gold;
And how they are safe through all the years
From sickness and want and war.
We thank the great God, with falling tears,
For the things in the cabinet drawer."

s: Others in the house might have slept, but she could not spare a moment of the precious time allotted to her with her little one, and all through the night she must have prayed that God would shield and protect her baby and bless the work she had done and the step she was about to take.
Some people often say to me: "I wonder what the angels do; how do they spend their time?"
I think I know what some of them were doing that night.
You can bet they were not off at some bridge-whist party.
They guarded that house so carefully that not one soldier of old Pharaoh ever crossed the threshold.
They saw to it that not one of them harmed that baby.

At dawn the mother must have kissed him good-bye, placed him in the ark and hidden him among the reeds and rushes, and with an aching heart and tear-dimmed eyes turned back again to the field and back to the brickyards to labor and to wait and see what God would do.
She had done her prayerful best, and when you have done that, you can bank on God to give the help you need.
If only we believed that with God all things are possible, no matter how unlikely, what unexpected answers the Lord would give to our prayers!
She knew God would help her somehow, but I don't think she ever dreamed that God would help her by sending Pharaoh's daughter to care for the child.
It was no harder for God to send the princess than it was to get the mother to prepare the ark.
What was impossible from her point of view was easy for God.
Pharaoh's daughter came down to the water to bathe, and the ark was discovered, just as God wanted it to be, and one of her maids was sent to bring it.
You often wonder what the angels are doing.
I think some of the angels kept the crocodiles herded on the other side of the Nile to keep them from finding Moses and eating him up.
You can bank on it: all heaven was concerned to see that not one hair of that baby's head was harmed.
There were not enough devils in hell to pull one hair out of its head.

The ark was brought, and with a woman's curiosity the daughter of Pharaoh had to look into it to see what was there, and when they removed the cover, there lay a strong, healthy baby boy, kicking up his heels and sucking his thumbs, as most of us probably did when we were boys, and as you probably did when you were a girl.
The baby looks up and weeps, and those tears blotted out all that was against it and gave it a chance for its life.
I don't know, but I think an angel stood there and pinched it to make it cry, for it cried at just the right time.
Just as God plans.
God always does things at the right time.
Give God a chance; He may be a little slow at times, but He will always get there in time.
The tears of that baby were the jewels with which Israel was ransomed from Egyptian bondage.
The princess had a woman's heart, and when a woman's heart and a baby's tears meet, something happens that gives the devil cold feet.
Perhaps the princess had had a baby who died, and the sight of Moses may have torn the wound open and made it bleed afresh.
But she had a woman's heart, and that made her forget she was the daughter of Pharaoh, and she was determined to give protection to that baby.
Faithful Miriam (the Lord be praised for Miriam) saw the heart of the princess reflected in her face.

Miriam had studied faces so much that she could read the princess's heart as plainly as if it were written in an open book, and she said to her: "Shall I go and get one of the Hebrew women to nurse the child for you?" And the princess said, "Go."
I see her little feet and legs fly as she runs down the hot, dusty road, and her mother must have seen her coming a mile away, and she ran to meet her and to have her own baby put back into her arms.
And she was being paid in Egyptian gold to take care of her own baby.
Do you see how the Lord does things?
"Now you take this child and nurse it for me, and I will pay you your wages."
It was a joke on Pharaoh's daughter, paying the mother of Moses for doing what she wanted to do more than anything else—nurse her own baby.

How quickly the mother was repaid for those long hours of anxiety and alarm and grief, and if the angels know what is going on, what a merry time there must have been in heaven when they saw Moses and Miriam back at home, under the protection of the daughter of Pharaoh!
I imagine she dropped to her knees and poured out her heart to God, who had helped her so gloriously.
She must have said: "Well, Lord, I knew You would help me.

I knew You would take care of my baby when I made the ark and put him in it and set it in the water, but I never dreamed that You would put him back into my arms to care for, so that I would not have to work and slave in the field and make bricks and be tortured almost to death for fear that the soldiers of Pharaoh would find my baby and kill him.
I never thought You would soften the stony heart of Pharaoh and make him pay me for what I would rather do than anything else in this world."
I expect to meet the mother of Moses in heaven, and I am going to ask her how much old Pharaoh had to pay her for that job.
I think that is one of the best jokes—that old sinner having to pay the mother to take care of her own baby.
But I tell you, if you give God a chance, He will fill your heart to overflowing.
Just give Him a chance.
This mother had remarkable pluck.
Everything was against her, but she would not give up.
Her heart never failed.
She fought as brave a fight as any man ever fought at the sound of the cannon or the roar of musketry.

blocks.x:
"The bravest battle that was ever fought,
Shall I tell you where and when?
On the maps of the world you will not find it—
It was fought by the mothers of men.

"No, not with cannon or battle shot,
With sword or noble pen,
No, not with the eloquent word or thought
From the mouths of wonderful men.

"But deep in the walled-up woman's heart—
Of women who would not yield,
But bravely, silently bore their part—
See, there is the battlefield.

"No marshaling troops, no bivouac song,
No banner to gleam and wave;
But oh, these battles, they last so long—
From babyhood to the grave."

s: Mothers are always brave when the safety of their children is at stake.
This incident took place out West.
A mother was working in a garden, and her little one was sitting under a tree in the yard, playing.

The mother heard the child scream; she ran, and a huge snake was wrapping its coils around the baby, and as its head swung around she leaped and seized it by the neck and tore it from her baby and hurled it against a tree.
Fathers frequently give up.

The old man often takes to boozing, becomes dissipated, takes a dose of poison and commits suicide; but the mother will stand by the home and keep the little band together, even if she has to manicure her fingernails over a washboard to do it.
If men had half as much grit as the women, there would be different stories written about a good many homes.
Look at her work!
It is the greatest in the world; in its far-reaching importance it rises transcendently above everything in the universe—her task of molding hearts and lives and shaping character.
If you want to find greatness, don't go to the throne; go to the cradle; and the nearer you get to the cradle, the nearer you get to greatness.
Now, when Jesus wanted to give His disciples an impressive object lesson, He called in a college professor, did He?
Hardly. He brought in a little child and said: "Unless you become as one of these, you shall by no means enter the kingdom of God."
The work is so important that God will not trust anybody with it but a mother.
The launching of a boy or a girl to live for Christ is a greater work than the launching of a battleship.
Moses was a chosen vessel of the Lord, and God wanted him to get the right kind of start, so He gave him a good mother.
There was not a college professor in all Egypt whom God would trust with that baby! So He put the child back into its mother's arms.
He knew that the best one on earth to trust with that baby was its own mother.
When God sends us great men, He wants them to get the right kind of start.
So He sees to it that they have a good mother.
Almost any old stick will do for a daddy.
God is particular about the mothers.
And so the great need of this country, or of any other country, is good mothers, and I believe we have more good mothers in America than any other nation on earth.
If Washington's mother had been like a Happy Hooligan's mother, Washington would have been a Happy Hooligan.
Somebody has said: "God could not be everywhere, so He gave us mothers."

Now, there may be poetry in it, but it is true "that the hand that rocks the cradle rules the world," and if every cradle were rocked by a good mother, the world would be full of good men, as sure as you breathe.
If every boy and every girl today had a good mother, the saloons and houses of ill repute would go out of business tomorrow.
A young man once joined a church, and the preacher asked him: "What was it I said that led you to become a Christian?"
The young man said: "Nothing that I ever heard you say; it was the way my mother lived."
I tell you, an ounce of example outweighs forty million tons of theory and speculation.
If mothers would live as they should, we preachers would have little to do.
Keep the devil out of the boys and girls, and he will get out of the world.
The old sinners will die off if we keep the young ones clean.
The biggest place in the world is the one being filled by the people who are closely in touch with youth.

Being a king, an emperor or a president is mighty small potatoes compared to being a mother or a teacher of children, whether in a public school or in a Sunday school, and they fill places so great that there is not an angel in heaven who would not gladly give a bushel of diamonds to boot to come down here and take their places.
Commanding an army is little more than sweeping a street or pounding an anvil compared with the training of a boy or girl.
The mother of Moses did more for the world than all the kings Egypt ever had.
To teach a child to love truth and hate a lie, to love purity and hate vice, is greater than inventing a flying machine that will take you to the moon before breakfast.
Without realizing it, you set in motion influences that will damn or bless the old universe and bring new worlds out of chaos and transform them for God.
A man sent a friend of mine some crystals and said: "One of these crystals, as large as a pinpoint, will give a distinguishable green hue to sixteen hogsheads of water."
Think of it! Power enough in an atom to tint sixteen hogsheads of water.
There is power in a word or an act to blight a boy and, through him, to curse a community.
There is power enough in a word to tint the life of that child so that it will become a power to lift the world to Jesus Christ.
Mothers will set in motion influences that will touch either heaven or hell.
Talk about greatness!
Oh, you wait until you reach the mountains of eternity; then read the mothers' names in God's hall of fame, and see what they have been in this world.
Wait until you see God's hall of fame; you will see women bent over the washtub there.

I want to tell you women that fooling away your time hugging and kissing a poodle dog, caressing a "Spitz," drinking society brandy-mash and cocktails, and playing cards, is mighty small business compared to molding the life of a child.
Tell me, where did Moses get his faith?
From his mother. Where did Moses get the backbone to say, "I will not be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter"?
He got it from his mother.
Where did Moses get the nerve to say, "Excuse me, please," to the pleasures of Egypt?
He got it from his mother.
You can bank on it: he didn't breathe it in from his dad.
Many a boy would have turned out better if his old dad had died before the boy was born.
You tell your boy to stay out of bad company.
Sometimes, when he walks down the street with his father, he is in the worst company in town.
His dad smokes, drinks and chews.
Moses got it from his mother.
He was learned in all the wisdom of Egypt, but that did not give him a swelled head.
When God wants to throw a world out into space, He is not concerned about it.
The first mile that world travels settles its course for eternity.
When God throws a child out into the world, He is mighty anxious that it gets a good start.
The Catholics are right when they say: "Give us the children until they are ten years old, and we do not care who has them after that."
The Catholics are not losing any sleep over losing men and women from their church membership.
It is the only church that has ever shown us the only sensible way to reach the masses—that is, by getting hold of the children.
That is the only way on God's earth that you will ever solve the problem of reaching the masses.
Get the boys and girls started right, and the devil will hang crape on his door and bank his fires, and hell will be for rent before the Fourth of July.
A friend of mine has a little girl whom she had to take to the hospital for an operation.
They thought she would be frightened, but she said: "I don't care, if mama will be there and hold my hand."

They prepared her for the operation, led her into the room, put her on the table, put the cone over her face and saturated it with ether, and she said: "Now, mama, take me by the hand and hold it, and I will not be afraid."
And the mother stood there and held her hand.
The operation was performed, and when she regained consciousness they said: "Bessie, weren't you afraid when they put you on the table?"
She said: "No, mama stood there and held my hand.
I was not afraid."
There is a mighty power in a mother's hand.
There is more power in a woman's hand than in a king's scepter.
And there is a mighty power in a mother's kiss—inspiration, courage, hope, ambition—in a mother's kiss.
One kiss made Benjamin West a painter, and the memory of it stayed with him all through life.
One kiss will drive away the fear in the dark and make the little one brave.
It will give strength where there is weakness.

I was in a town one day and saw a mother out with her boy, and he had great steel braces on both legs, up to his hips, and when I got near enough to them I learned from their conversation that this was not the first time the mother had taken him out for a walk.
She had him out exercising so that he would get the use of his limbs.
He was struggling, and she smiled and said: "You are doing well today; better than you did yesterday."
And she stooped and kissed him, and the kiss of encouragement made him work all the harder, and she said: "You are doing nobly, son."
And he said: "Mama, I'm going to run; watch me."
And he started, and one of his toes caught on the steel brace on the other leg and he stumbled, but she caught him and kissed him and said: "That was fine, son; how well you did it!"
Now, he did it because his mother had encouraged him with a kiss.
He did not do it to show off.
There is nothing that will help and inspire a life like a mother's kiss.

blocks.x:
"If we knew the baby fingers pressed against the windowpane
Would be cold and still tomorrow, never to trouble us again,
Would the bright eyes of our darling catch the frown upon our brow?

"Let us gather up the sunbeams lying all around our path,
Let us keep the wheat and roses, casting out the thorns and chaff!
We shall find our sweetest comforts in the blessings of today,
With a patient hand removing all the briers from our way."

s: There is power in a mother's song, too.
It is the best music the world has ever heard.
The best music in the world is like biscuits—it is the kind mother makes.
There is no brass band or pipe organ that can hold a candle to mother's song.
Calvé, Melba, Nordica, Eames, Schumann-Heink—they are cheap skates compared to mother.
They cannot sing at all.
They do not know the rudiments of the kind of music mother sings.
The kind she sings gets tangled up in your heartstrings.
The music of heaven would be a disappointment to me if there were no mothers there to sing.
The song of an angel or a seraph would not have much charm for me.
What would you care for an angel's song if there were no mother's song?
The song of a mother is sweeter than any ever sung by minstrel or written by poet.
Talk about sonnets! You ought to hear a mother sing when her baby is at her breast, when her heart is filled with emotion.
Her voice may not please an artist, but it will please anyone who has a heart in him.
The songs that have moved the world are not the songs written by the great masters.
The best music, in my judgment, is not the flawless performance of these high-priced opera singers.
There is nothing in art that can put into melody the happiness that associations and memories bring.
I think that when we reach heaven we will find that some of the best songs we sing there will be those we learned at mother's knee.
There is power in a mother's love.
A mother's love must be like the love of God.
How God could ever have told the world that He loved it without a mother's help has often puzzled me.
If the devils in hell ever turned pale, it was on the day a mother's love flamed up for the first time in a woman's heart.
If the devil ever got "cold feet," it was that day, in my judgment.
You know, a mother has to love her baby before it is born.

Like God, she has to go into the shadows of the valley of death to bring it into the world, and she will love her child and suffer for it, and it can grow up and become vile, and yet she will love it.
Nothing will make her blame it, and I think, women, that one of the awful things in hell will be that there will be no mother's love there.
Nothing but black, bottomless, endless, eternal hate in hell—no mother's love.

blocks.x:
"And though he creeps through the vilest caves of sin,
And crouches, perhaps, with bleary and bloodshot eyes,
Under the hangman's rope—a mother's lips
Will kiss him in his last bed of disgrace,
And love him even for what she hoped of him."

s: I thank God for what a mother's love has done for the world.
Oh, there is power in a mother's trust.
Just as surely as Moses was put into his mother's arms by the princess, so God has put the babies into your arms, as a charge from Him to raise and care for.
Every child is put into a mother's arms as a trust from God, and she has to answer to God for the way she deals with that child.
No mother on God's earth has any right to raise her children for pleasure.
She has no right to send them to dancing school and to haunts of sin.
You have no right to do those things that will curse your children.
That baby is put into your arms to be trained for the Lord.
No mother has any more right to raise her children for pleasure than I have to pick your pockets or throw red pepper in your eyes.
She has no more right to do that than a bank cashier has to rifle the vaults and take the savings of the people.
One of the worst sins you can commit is to be unfaithful to your trust.
"Take this child and nurse it for me."
That is all the business you have with it.
That is a jewel that belongs to God, and He gives it to you to polish for Him so He can set it in a crown.
Who knows but that Judas became the godless, good-for-nothing wretch he was because he had a godless, good-for-nothing mother?
Do you know? I do not.
What is more to blame for the crowded prisons than mothers?

Who is more to blame for the crowded houses of ill repute than you are, who let your children gad about the streets with every Tom, Dick and Harry, or keep company with some little jack rabbit whose character would make a black mark on a piece of tar paper?
I have talked with men in prisons who have damned their mothers to my face.
Why? They blame their mothers for their being where they are.
"Take the child and nurse it for me, and I will pay you your wages."
God pays in joy that is fireproof, famine-proof and devil-proof.
He will pay you; don't you worry.
So get your name on God's payroll.
"Take this child and nurse it for me, and I will pay you your wages."
If you have not been doing that, then get your name on God's payroll.
"Take this child and nurse it for me, and I will pay you your wages."
Then there is your responsibility! It is so great that I do not see how any woman can fail to be a Christian and serve God.
What do you think God will do if the mother fails?
I stagger under it.
What if, through your unfaithfulness, your boy becomes a curse and your daughter a blight?
What if, through your neglect, that boy becomes a Judas when he might have been a John or a Paul?
Down in Cincinnati some years ago a mother went to the zoological garden and stood leaning over the bear pit, watching the bears and dropping crumbs and peanuts to them.
In her arms she held her baby, a year and three months old.
She was so absorbed in the bears that the baby wriggled out of her arms and fell into the bear pit, and she watched those huge monsters rip it to shreds.
What a veritable hell it will be all through her life to know that her little one was lost through her own carelessness and neglect!
"Take this child and raise it for me, and I will pay you your wages."
Will you promise and covenant with God, and with me, and with one another, that from now on you will try, with God's help, to do better than you ever have done in raising your children for God?

"I once read the story of an angel who stole out of heaven and came to this world one bright, sunshiny day; he roamed through field, forest, city and village, and as the sun went down he preened his wings for the return flight.
The angel said: "Now that my visit is over, before I return I must gather some mementos of my trip."

He looked at the beautiful flowers in the garden and said, "How lovely and fragrant," and he plucked the rarest roses, made a bouquet, and said: "I see nothing more beautiful and fragrant than these flowers."

The angel looked farther and saw a bright-eyed, rosy-cheeked child, and said: "That baby is prettier than the flowers; I will take that, too." And looking behind to the cradle, he saw a mother's love pouring out over her baby like a gushing spring, and the angel said: "The mother's love is the most beautiful thing I have seen!
I will take that, too."
And with these three treasures the heavenly messenger winged his flight to the pearly gates, saying: "Before I go, I must examine the mementos of my trip to the earth."
He looked at the flowers; they had withered.
He looked at the baby's smile, and it had faded.
He looked at the mother's love, and it shone in all its original beauty.

Then he threw away the withered flowers, cast aside the faded smile, and, with the mother's love pressed to his breast, swept through the gates into the city, shouting that the only thing he had found that would keep its fragrance from earth to heaven was a mother's love.
"Take this child and nurse it for me, and I will pay you your wages."
When Napoleon Bonaparte was asked, "What do you regard as the greatest need of France?" he replied, "Mothers, mothers, mothers."
You women can make a hell of a home or a heaven of a home.
Don't turn your old Gatling-gun tongue loose and rip everybody up, and rip up your husbands and send them out of their homes.
If I were going to investigate your piety, I would ask the girl who works for you.
This talk about the land of the free counts for little when the children look like a rummage sale in a secondhand store, with uncombed hair, ripped pants, buttons off and stockings hanging down.
It does not take the wisdom of truth to see that mother is too busy with her social duties, clubs and so on to pay much attention to the kids.
The mother of Nero was a murderess, and it is no wonder that he fiddled while Rome burned.
The mother of Patrick Henry was eloquent, and that is the reason every schoolboy and schoolgirl knows, "Give me liberty or give me death."
Coleridge's mother taught him Bible stories from the old Dutch tiles of the fireplace.
Authority in the home is needed today more than at any time in the history of this nation.
I have met in the arena of conflict every form of man and beast one could imagine meeting, and I am convinced that neither law nor gospel can make a nation without home authority and home example.
These two things are needed.
The boy who has a wholesome home and surroundings, with sensible discipline included, does not often find his way into the reformatory.
Susanna Wesley was the mother of nineteen children, and she held them for God.
When asked how she did it, she replied, "By getting hold of their hearts in their youth, and never losing my grip."

If it had not been for the earnest protests of the mother of George Washington, George Washington would have become a midshipman in the British navy, and the name of that capital over there would have been something else.
John Randolph said in the House of Representatives, "If it had not been for my godly mother, I, John Randolph, would have been an infidel."
Gray, who wrote the "Elegy in a Country Churchyard," said he was one of a large family of children who had the misfortune to outlive their mother.
And I believe the ideal mother is the product of a civilization that rose from the manger of Bethlehem.
I am sure there is not an angel in heaven who would not be glad to come to earth and be honored with motherhood, if God would grant that privilege.

What a grand thing it must be, at the end of your earthly career, to look back upon a noble and godly life, knowing that you did all you could to help leave this old world to God, that you made your contributions in tears and in prayers, and that you taught your offspring to be God-fearing, so that when you were gone you would go on reproducing your noble character in your children.

I believe in blood; I believe in good blood, bad blood, honest blood and thieving blood; in heroic blood and cowardly blood; in virtuous blood, in licentious blood, in drinking blood and in sober blood.

The lips of the Hapsburgs tell of licentiousness; those of the Stuarts tell of cruelty, bigotry and sensuality, from Mary, Queen of Scots, down to Charles the First and Charles the Second, and James the First—who showed the world what your fool of a Scotsman can be when he is a fool—down to King James the Second.
Scottish blood stands for stubbornness.
They are full of stick-to-itiveness.
I know; Mrs. Sunday is full-blooded Scottish.
English blood speaks of reverence for the English.
That is shown by the fact that England recently spent $50,000,000 to put a crown on George's head.
Danish blood tells of a love of the sea.
Welsh blood tells of religious fervor and zeal for God.
Jewish blood tells of a love of money, from the days of Abraham down until now.
You may have read this story: down in New York there was a woman who said to her drunken son, "Let's go down to the police court and have the judge send you over to the island for a few weeks.
Maybe you will straighten up then, and I can have some respect for you again."
Down they went to the police court and appeared before the judge.
He asked who would make the charge, and the mother sprang forward with the words on her lips.
Then she stopped short, turned to her son and, throwing her arms around his neck, cried out, "I can't!
I can't! He is my son; I love him, and I can't."
Then she fell dead at his feet.
As dearly as she loved her drunken, bloated, loafing son, she could not stand in judgment over him.
"Therefore I say to you, all manner of sin and blasphemy will be forgiven men: but the blasphemy against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven men.
"And whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man, it will be forgiven him: but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven him, neither in this world nor in the world to come."
I would like to know where anyone ever found any authority for a belief in a probation after death.
Jesus Christ was either human or He was divine.
And if He was only human, then I am no more obligated to obey His word than I am that of any other philosopher.
The Pharisees charged Jesus with being in league with the devil.
They said to Him, "You have a devil."
They grew bolder in their denunciation and said, "You do what You do through Beelzebub, the prince of devils."
Jesus said, "How can that be?
If I do what I do through the devil, explain why I am overthrowing the works of the devil.
If I am a devil, and if what I do is through the devil, then I would not be working to harm the works of the devil.
I would not be doing what I am doing to destroy the works of the devil, but I would be working to destroy the works of God."
From that day on they did not dare ask Him any more questions.
I know that men hold various opinions as to what they believe constitutes the sin against the Holy Spirit.
There are those who think it could have been committed only by those who heard Jesus Christ speak and saw Him in the flesh.
If that is true, then neither you nor I are in danger, for neither of us has ever seen Jesus in the flesh or heard Him.

Another group thinks that it has been committed since the days of Jesus, but only at extremely rare intervals; and still a third group thinks they have committed it, and they spend their lives in gloom and dread and are completely useless to themselves and to the community.

And yet I have not the slightest doubt that there are thousands who come under the heading of my message who are never gloomy, never depressed, never downcast; their conscience is at ease, their spirits are light and cheerful, they eat three meals a day and sleep as soundly as a baby at night; nothing seems to disturb them, and life is all pleasure and song.

If you will lay aside any preconceived ideas or opinions that you may have had, or still have, about what you imagine, think or believe constitutes the sin against the Holy Spirit, or the unpardonable sin, and if you will listen to me—for I have read every sermon on the subject I could ever get my hands on, and have listened to every man I have ever had an opportunity to hear preach, and have read everything the Bible teaches on the subject.

I do not say that my views on the subject are infallible, but I have wept and prayed and studied over it, and if time permits and my strength allows and your patience endures, I will try to ask and answer a few questions.
What is it? Why will God not forgive it?
It is not swearing.
If swearing were the unpardonable sin, lots of men in heaven would have to go to hell, and there are multitudes on earth on their way to heaven who would have to go to hell.
It is not drunkenness.
There are multitudes in heaven who have crept and crawled out of the swamps of filth and the cesspools of wickedness and drunkenness.
Some of the brightest lights that ever blazed for God have been men whom God saved from drunkenness.
It is not adultery. Jesus said to the woman who was committing adultery and was caught in the very act, "Neither do I condemn you; go and sin no more."
It is not theft. He said to Zaccheus, "Today salvation has come to your house."
Zaccheus had been a thief.
It is not murder. Men's hands have been red with blood, and God has forgiven them.
The apostle Paul's hands were red with blood.
What is it? To me it is plain and simple.
It is the constant and continual, and final, rejection of Jesus Christ as your Savior.
God's offer of mercy and salvation comes to you, and you say, "No," and you push it aside.
I do know that there is such a thing as a last call to every man or woman.
God says that His Spirit will not always strive with man, and when a man or woman says "No" as God's Spirit strives for the last time, it seals your doom forever.
It is no special form of sin, no single act.
It might be swearing; it might be theft.

Any sin becomes unpardonable if God keeps calling on you to forsake it and you keep refusing to forsake it; and if you do not, then He will withdraw and leave you alone, and that sin will become unpardonable, for God will not ask you again to forsake it.
It is not one glaring act, but the constant repetition of the same thing.
There will come a time when you commit that sin once too often.
It is a known law of the mind that truth resisted loses its power over the mind that resists it.
You hear a truth the first time and reject it.
The next time the truth will not seem so strong, and it will be easier to resist.
God throws a truth in your face.
You reject it. He throws it again; you reject it again.
Finally God will stop throwing the truth at you, and you will have committed the unpardonable sin.

s: Over in Scotland there are men who earn their living by gathering the eggs of birds laid on ledges of rock far below the top of the cliff.
They fasten a rope to a tree and also to themselves, then swing back and forth and in onto the ledge of rock.
When a man was doing that very thing years ago, the rope beneath his arms came untied, and the jutting rock caused the rope to hang many feet beyond his reach.
The man waited for help to come, but none came.
Darkness came, then day dawned, and he gave himself up to the fate of starvation, which he felt was inevitably awaiting him, when a breeze freshened and the dangling rope began to sway.

As the wind increased in speed, it increased the swaying of the rope, and as it swung in, he said, "If I miss it, I die; if I seize it, it is my only chance," and with a prayer to God, as the rope swung in, he leaped out over the chasm and seized it and made his way hand over hand to the top, and when he reached it his hair was as white as the driven snow.
There is one cord that swings through this old world today—the Holy Spirit.
With every invitation it swings farther away.
We are living in the last dispensation, the dispensation of the Holy Spirit, and God is speaking to the world through the Holy Spirit today.
By every known law of the mind, conversion must be brought about by the influence of the truth on the mind.
Every time you resist the truth, the next time you hear it, it loses its force on your mind.
And every time you hear a truth and withstand it, you become stronger in your power to resist the truth.
We all know this: each resistance strengthens you against the truth.
When a man hears the truth and resists it, the truth grows weaker and he grows stronger to resist it.
No matter what Jesus Christ did, the Jews refused to believe.

He had performed wonderful deeds, but they would not believe; so when Lazarus was dead, He said, "Lazarus, come forth," and then turned to the Jews and said, "Isn't that evidence enough that I am the Son of God?" and they cried, "Away with Him."
One day He was walking down the hot, dusty road and He met a funeral procession.
The mourners were carrying the body of a young man, and his mother was weeping.
He told them to set the coffin on the ground and said:
"Young man, arise," and he arose.
Then He asked the Pharisees, "Is that not proof enough that I am the Son of God, that I make the dead rise?" and they cried, "Away with Him."
So no matter what Jesus did, the Jews refused to believe Him.
No matter what Jesus Christ says or does today, you will refuse to accept, and you will go on rushing headlong to eternal damnation.
Jesus Christ gives you just as much evidence today.
Down in Indiana, my friend Mrs. Robinson was preaching.
I do not remember the town, but I think it was Kokomo; and I remember the incident, and how on the last day she tried to get the leader of society there to give her heart to God.
She preached and then went down into the aisle and talked to her.
Then she went back to the platform and made her appeal from there.
Again she went to the girl, but she still refused.
As Mrs. Robinson turned to go, she saw her borrow a pencil from her escort and write something in the back of a hymnbook.
A few years afterward Mrs. Robinson went back to the town and was told that the girl was dying.
They told her the physicians had just held a consultation and said she could not live until night.
Mrs. Robinson hurried to her home.
The girl looked up, recognized her and said, "I didn't send for you.
You came on your own account, and you are too late."
To every appeal she would reply, "You are too late."
Finally she said, "Go look in the hymnbook in the church."
They hurried to the church and looked through the hymnbooks and found in the back of one her name and address and these words: "I'll run the risk; I'll take my chance."
That was the last call to her.
No single sin is the unpardonable sin, but it may be that constant repetition, over and over again, until God will say, "Take it and go to hell."
Who can commit it?
I used to think that only the vile and the profane were the people who could commit it.
Whom did Jesus warn?
The Pharisees. And who were they?
The best men, morally, in Jerusalem.
Who can commit it?
Any man or woman who says "No" to Jesus Christ.
You may even defend the Bible.
You may be the best man or woman, morally, in the world.

Your name may be synonymous with virtue and purity, but let God try to get into your heart, let Him try to get you to walk down the aisle and publicly acknowledge Jesus Christ, and your heart and lips are sealed like a bank vault, and God has not been able to pull you to your feet.
And God will not keep on begging you to do it.
Something may say to you, "I ought to be a Christian."
This is the dispensation of the Holy Spirit.
God has spoken in three dispensations.
First, through the old Mosaic law.
Then Jesus Christ came upon this earth and lived, and the Jews and Gentiles conspired to kill Him.
Then the Holy Spirit came down at Pentecost, and God is speaking through the Holy Spirit today.
The Holy Spirit is pressing you to be a Christian.

It takes the combined efforts of the Trinity to keep you out of hell—God the Father to provide the plan of salvation, the Holy Spirit to convict, Jesus Christ to redeem you through His blood, and your acceptance and repentance to save you.
Sin is no trifle.
The only representative of the Trinity in the world today is the Holy Spirit.
Jesus has been here, but He is not here now—that is, in flesh and blood.
The Holy Spirit is here now.
When He leaves the world, good-bye.
There was an old saint of God, now in glory.
He was holding meetings one time, and a young man came down the aisle and went so far as to ask him to pray for him.
He said, "Let's settle it now," but the young man refused and told him to pray for him.
Years afterward, in Philadelphia, the old saint was in a hotel, waiting for his card to be taken up to the man he wanted to see.
He looked in at the barroom door.
There was a young man ordering a drink.
The two saw each other's reflections in the French plate glass behind the bar, and the young man came out and said, "How do you do?"
The old man spoke to him.
The young fellow said, "I suppose you don't remember me?" and the old saint had to admit that he did not.
The young fellow asked him if he remembered the meeting eleven years before in New York when a young man came down the aisle and asked him to pray for him.
He said he was that young man.
The old saint said, "From what I have just seen, I would suppose that you did not settle it."
The young fellow said, "I did not, and I never expect to.
I believe there is a hell, and I'm going there as fast as I can go."
The old man begged him to be quiet, but he said, "It is true.
If Jesus Christ came through that door now, I would spit in His face."
The old man said, "Don't talk that way.
I would not stand for you to talk about my wife that way, and I will not stand for you to talk about Christ that way."
The young fellow said it was all true.
The old fellow said, "Maybe it is all true, but I do not like to hear it."
The young fellow said it was true, and that if he had a Bible he would tear it up.
With a string of oaths he went to the bar, took two or three drinks and went out the door.
Sometimes it may be utter, absolute indifference.
Some can hear any sermon and any song and not be moved.
I will venture that some of you have not been convicted of sin for twenty-five years.
Back then the Spirit of God convicted you, and you did not yield.
The first place I ever preached, in the little town of Garner, in Hancock County, Iowa, a man came down the aisle.
I said, "Who's that?" and someone told me that he was one of the richest men in the county.
I asked him what I had said to help him, and he said nothing.
Then he told me that twenty-one years before he had gone to Chicago and sold his stock four hours before he had to catch a train.
Moody was in town, and with a friend he had gone and stood inside the door, listening to the sermon.
When Moody gave the invitation, he handed his coat and hat to his friend and said he was going down to give Moody his hand.
The friend told him not to do it, that he would miss his train, and then the railroad pass would be no good after that day.
He said he could afford to pay his way home.
His friend told him not to go up there amid all the excitement, but to wait and settle it at home.
He said he had waited thirty-five years and had not settled it at home, but the friend kept insisting that he not go forward and give his heart to God.
Finally the time passed and they had to catch the train, and the man had not gone forward.
He told me that he had never had a desire to give his heart to God until that time, twenty-one years later, when he heard me preach.
The Spirit called him when he heard Moody, and then the Spirit did not call him again until twenty-one years later, when he heard me.
I have never said, and I never will say, that all unbelievers died in agony.
A man ordinarily dies as he has lived.
If you have lived in unbelief, in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred you will die that way.
If Christianity is a good thing to die with, it is a good thing to live with.
I don't put much stock in these deathbed confessions.
A deathbed confession is like burning a candle at both ends and then blowing the smoke in the face of Jesus.
A deathbed confession is like drinking the cup of life and then offering the dregs to Christ.

I think it is one of the most contemptible, miserable, low-down, unmanly and unwomanly things you can do, to keep your life in your own control until the last moment and then try to creep into the kingdom on account of the long-suffering and mercy of Jesus Christ.
I do not say that none is genuine.
But there is only one on record in the Bible, and that was the first time the dying thief had ever heard of Christ, and he accepted at once.
So your case is not comparable to this.
You have had wagonloads of sermons dumped into you, but it is a mighty hard thing to accept in the last moment.

If you have lived without conviction, your friends ought not to get angry when the preacher preaches your funeral sermon if he does not put you in the front row in heaven, with a harp in your hands and a crown on your head.
God can forgive sins, but you have to comply with His requirements.
He is not willing that any should perish, but He has a right to tell you and me what to do to be saved.
A doctor had been in practice for sixty years, and he was asked how many godless men he had seen show any trace of concern on their deathbed.
He said he had kept track of three hundred, and only three had shown any real concern.
That is appalling to me.
You ordinarily die as you have lived.
A minister was called to a house of shame to be with a dying girl in her last moments.
He prayed and then looked at her face and saw no signs of hope of repentance.

He was led to pray again, and this time he was led to put in a verse of Scripture, Isaiah 1:18: "Come now, and let us reason together, says the Lord: Though your sins are as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they are red like crimson, they shall be as wool."
"Is that what the Bible says?" the girl asked.
He said it was.
"Would you let me see it?" And the minister pointed it out to her.
"Would you pray again and put in that verse?" the girl asked, and as he started she called out, "Stop!
Let me put my finger on that verse."
The minister prayed, and when he looked again he saw hope and pardon and peace in the girl's face.
"I'm so glad God made that 'scarlet,'" she said, "for that means me."
All manner of sins God will forgive.
Then tell me why you will not come when God says, "All manner of sin and blasphemy will be forgiven men."
Great heavens! I can't understand how you can sit still.
But a man says, "Bill, will He forgive a murderer?
My hands are red with blood, although no one knows it."
Didn't I say He forgave Paul?
A friend of mine was preaching in Lansing, Michigan, one time, and in the middle section of the church there was a man who made him so nervous that he could not watch him and preach.

Nothing seemed to catch his attention until my friend said, "Suppose there were a murderer here tonight; God would forgive him if he accepted Christ," and at the word murderer the man grabbed the chair in front of him and sat rigid throughout the sermon, never taking his eyes off my friend.
At the end of the meeting my friend went down to him and asked him what was the matter, telling him that he had made him so nervous he could hardly preach.
The man said, "I'm a murderer.
I got off on a technicality, and I'm supporting the widow and children, but I am a murderer."
My friend brought him to Jesus Christ, and now that man is a power in the Church.
All manner of sins God says He will forgive.
Some say, "Mr. Sunday, why is it that so few aged sinners are converted?"
Infidels, when asked this, seize upon it as a plan of attack.
When God begins to show His power, then the devil and all the demons of hell get busy.
That is the best evidence in the world that these meetings are doing good, when that bunch of knockers gets busy.

Infidels sneer and say, "How does it happen that when a man's mind has developed through age and experience and contact with the world, and he has passed the period of youthful enthusiasm—how does it happen that so few of them are converted?"
Religion makes its appeal to your feelings, not to your intellect.
The way into the kingdom of heaven is heart first, not head first.
God is not an explanation; God is a revelation.
A grain of corn is a revelation, but you can't explain it.
You know that if you put the plant kingdom into the mineral kingdom, the plant will be born again, but you can't explain it.
Some of the greatest things are revelations.
Therefore, instead of being an argument against religion, it is an argument for it.
Don't you know that sixteen out of twenty who are converted are converted before they are twenty years old?
Don't you know that eighteen out of thirty who are converted are converted before they are thirty years old?
Don't you know that?
What does that prove?
It proves that if you are not converted before you are thirty years old, the chances are about 100,000 to one that you never will be converted.
Most people are converted at special revival services.
I want to hurl this in the teeth and cram it down the throats of those who sneer at revival efforts—preachers included.
Almost nine-tenths of the Christians at this meeting were converted at a revival.
What does that show?
It shows that if you are thirty and have not been converted, the chances are that if you are not converted at this revival you never will be converted.
If it were not for revivals, just think what hell would be like.
Then think of any low-down, God-forsaken, dirty gang knocking a revival.
God says, "You can spurn My love and trample the blood under your feet, but if you seek My pardon I will forgive you."
You may have been indifferent to the appeals of the minister; you may have been a thief, or an adulterer, or a blasphemer, or a scoffer, and all that; but God says, "I will forgive you."
You may have been indifferent to the tears of your poor wife and children and friends, but if you will seek God, He will forgive you.
But when He came down and revealed Himself as the Son of God through the Holy Spirit, if you sneer and say it is not true, your sin may become unpardonable.
If you do not settle it here, you will never settle it anywhere else.
I will close with a word of comfort and a word of warning.
If you have a desire to be a Christian, it is proof that the devil has not got you yet.
That is the comfort.
Now for the warning: if you have that desire, thank God for it and yield to it.
You may never have another chance.
Lord, is it I?—Matthew 26:22.

God created man and placed him in the Garden of Eden, and gave him an explicit command, and man disobeyed, with full knowledge of the penalty ringing in his ears, for God said: "On the day you eat of the fruit, you will surely die."
The Lord did not mean a period of twenty-four hours, but He did mean that man would pass through a crisis in his career.
Adam ate the forbidden fruit, and this world became a graveyard.
If man had not sinned, we would never have died.
All the misery, all the disease, and all the heartaches have come through sin.
The hearse backs up in front of our homes and drives away with our loved ones, because of sin.
But when man sinned, God gave the promise, "The seed of the woman shall bruise the serpent's head."
In the fullness of time Jesus came into the world in fulfillment of that promise.
He opened the eyes of the blind, calmed the storm, fed the multitude with five loaves and two fish, cast out demons, and raised the dead.
He demonstrated by word and deed that He was the Son of God.
The Jews spurned and rejected His claim, and their hostility finally culminated in His crucifixion.
But before that heartrending tragedy was carried out, several incidents took place, and from one of them I take my text.
Jesus said to His disciples, "Go your way into the village across from you, and you will find a colt tied there that no man has ever sat on; untie him and bring him to Me.
And if any man asks you, 'Why are you doing this?' say, 'The Lord needs him,' and right away he will send him here."

And the disciples went their way and found the colt tied in front of a house where two roads met, and there was a crowd of men loafing about the place; and if they were anything like the bunch in our day, they were whittling, cursing, chewing tobacco, and discussing financial, political and all other public questions.
The disciples began untying the colt, when one fellow, who spits enough tobacco juice to drown a rabbit, calls out, "Hey there!
What are you doing?
What are you going to do with that colt?"
The disciples call back: "The Lord needs him."
So away they go with the colt to where Jesus was, and He, seated on its back, enters the city of Jerusalem in His famous triumphal entry.
A great multitude followed, shouting, "Hosanna to the Son of David!
Blessed is He that comes in the name of the Lord!"
They spread their garments on the ground in front of Jesus.
They cut down branches from the trees; they paved His way with flowers.
You would have thought from their acclaim that then and there they would crown Him, but let us wait and see.
Jesus said to Peter and John, "Go on ahead, and you will meet a man carrying a pitcher of water.
Follow him into the house he enters, and say to the head of the house, 'Where is the guest room?'
He will show you an upper room, furnished; make preparations there."

Jesus desired to eat the Passover feast with His disciples, commemorating the passing over of the destroying angel, who went throughout the land of Egypt and killed the firstborn in every home where the blood was not on the doorposts.
That night at the table Peter noticed that Jesus looked sad and troubled.
Turning to John, who was one of the favored disciples, he said, "Ask Him what the matter is."
John said, "Master, you look worried.
Why is that?" Jesus replied: "One of you shall betray Me."
Peter asked, in the words of my text: "Lord, is it I?"
John also asked: "Lord, is it I?"
And Judas, the arch-traitor, had the nerve and the audacity to look Jesus in the face and ask: "Lord, is it I?"
And this when for days he had been bartering and haggling to betray Jesus to the Pharisees for thirty pieces of silver—about fifteen dollars and ninety-five cents in our money.
Jesus replied: "It is he to whom I give the morsel."
Saying this, He dipped it in the dish and handed the morsel to Judas, saying: "Whatever you are doing, do it quickly."
Stung to the heart by the words of Jesus, Judas leaped to his feet, and because he was treasurer of the little apostolic band, he seized the money bag and left the room.
And when they had sung a hymn, Jesus, with the remaining eleven disciples, went out, crossed the brook Kidron, and entered the Garden of Gethsemane.
This brings me to the subject of my sermon: The Three Groups in the Garden.
They were not grouped by their rating with Bradstreet or Dun.
Every man classified himself—and you do the same.
You are where you are because Jesus knows He cannot trust you in a more responsible place.
Judas classified himself with the enemies of God.
The first group was near the edge of the garden; the second group farther into the garden; while Jesus, we are told, was a stone's throw farther on.
The first group of disciples was so near the edge of the garden that they would have had only a short distance to go to be outside, where Judas was with the scribes, the Pharisees and the mob.
I am sorry to say it, but it is the truth.
The truth is not always pleasant to hear, but it is profitable for all who will profit by the truth.
The first group corresponds to the position of a large percentage of members in the average church today.
They live such a selfish, indifferent, apathetic, "good Lord, good devil," milk-and-chalk, cider-and-vinegar sort of life that it is hard to tell whether they are in the church or in the world.
I detest any man who will trim his sails to catch a passing breeze of popularity and fight under a doubtful flag.
I love to see a person come out clearly for God without compromise.
The nearer the relationship, the stronger the ties of obligation.
I owe to Mrs. Sunday and our children what I do not owe to any other woman or children in the world, because of my relationship to them.
You owe to your wife and children what you do not owe to any other beings.
I owe to Jesus what I do not owe to the world.
I testify of the world that its deeds are evil.
I do not care whether they hiss me or applaud me, whether they dine me or damn me.
Jesus said: "The world will hate you as it hates Me."
"Woe to you when everyone speaks well of you."
One of the most uncomplimentary things that can be said at your funeral is that you had no enemies.
If you live an uncompromising life for Christ, you will have enemies.
The nearer the relationship, the greater the provocation.
I could in one act break my wife's heart and bring disgrace upon my children, but that act would not bring a tear to your eye.
Why? Because all the interest you have in me is that I may entertain or instruct you, and perhaps your concern ends there.
I have imagined that the conduct of multitudes who are in the church must almost break the heart of Christ.

God has the right to say, "I did not send My Son into the world to bathe it in blood and tears, and to open His veins with the cruel instrument of the cross, in order to redeem you to serve the flesh and the devil, but to serve Me.
I want your influence, your time, your money, your prayers, your tears."
Alexander the Great was once asked to take part in the Olympic games.
He replied: "I will, if kings are to be my opponents on the race track."
If we were found doing nothing in this world that is out of harmony with our birth from above, we would move this old sin-soaked world toward God.
You cannot do as you please.
The higher you climb, the more plainly you are seen.
When you are away from home, do not forget that God is everywhere.
When the son of Fulvius was discovered among the conspirators of Catiline, his old father rebuked him, saying: "I did not father you to serve Catiline, but to serve your country—Rome!"
You are redeemed by the precious blood of Christ, not to serve the world, but to serve God.

I love to see people as loyal to Jesus as Speaker Lenthall was to the Constitution in the days of King Charles I. When commanded to dissolve Parliament, he said: "I have neither eyes to see, ears to hear, nor tongue to speak, except as the Constitution, whose servant I am, is pleased to direct me."
Or as loyal as Prince William of Orange was to the Netherlands in the thirty-seven years of war.
King Philip of Spain offered him fabulous sums to surrender.

Prince William sent back the message that has become inlaid like a mosaic in the hearts of the Dutch people: "Not for life nor wife, nor children, nor lands would I mix in my cup one drop of the poison of treason!"
No wonder that when he was slain by the hand of an assassin, little children stopped playing and cried.
Many of our churches are not much more than mere social organizations.
They spend more time developing along social lines than along spiritual lines.
Businessmen and influential church members do not do their duty; they are completely wrapped up in their own affairs.
They are busy with the pursuits and frivolities of the world, and they lose the track.
The old-time fire and the old-time spirit are missing.
What can we expect from a social club other than a leading away from God?
Our churches need more of God, and less of dress, striving after wealth, and social life.
A woman in a western city went to her pastor and asked: "What can I do to win my husband to Christ?"
He answered: "You cannot win anyone to Christ the way you live."
She hung her head in shame and went home.
When her husband and her son, a young man of eighteen, came home, she said to them: "I wish you would stay a little while after dinner.
I want to speak with you."

They stepped into the parlor, and she put an arm around each of them and said: "I have not been a consistent Christian, and so I feel I have not been as good a wife to you, husband, or as good a mother to you, son, as I should have been.
Will you join me in praying that God will forgive me?"
All three of them knelt, and she tried to pray, but all she could say was, "O God!
O God!" But the Spirit broke up the fountains of the deep, and all three wept.
A few days later her husband publicly accepted Christ and joined the church.

"Husband, tell me why I could not win you to Christ before," she asked, and he said: "I would ask you to go with me to the theater, and you would go; to the dance, and you would go; to play cards, and you would.
You drank wine with me.
Then you would ask me to go to church with you, and to prayer meeting, and I would go.
You went where I went, and I went where you went.
You did what I did, and I did what you did.
In what way was your life any better than mine?"
To be able to convict others of sin, we must first get right with God ourselves.
Eight in the first group.
Three in the second group.
Jesus alone makes up the third.
The largest number in the first group.
Farthest from Jesus. Nearest to the world.
That has always been true of every church I have known anything about.
Ask the minister for a list of his members; then sit down and check off the prayer-meeting members.
You will find the largest number nearer to the card party and the wine supper—closer to the world than to the cross of Christ.
Someone said to Daniel Webster when he was a boy: "What are you going to be when you are a man?"
"A lawyer," he replied.
"But the profession is overcrowded."
Webster answered: "There is plenty of room at the top."
The nearer you get to Jesus, the more elbow room you will have and the smaller the crowd.
The most glorious exploits do not always give us the clearest index of the vices or virtues of men and women.
Sometimes a word, an act, a gesture, your absence or your presence, will give a clearer insight into your manhood or womanhood, or the lack of both, than some deed of bravery or feat of prowess.
Let us talk with Jesus for a minute.
"Jesus, how many disciples do you have?"
"I had twelve. I have only eleven now."
"Where is the missing one?"
"He has gone to betray Me."
"And yet, with eleven left, you are praying all alone?"
Just like many a minister with hundreds of members, bearing the burden all alone.
Judas bought a ticket to hell for thirty pieces of silver, and it was not a round-trip ticket either.
Let us go and talk with the eight:
"Where is Jesus?" "We do not know."
"Where are Peter, James and John?"
"Don't know; we haven't seen them."
"Where is Judas?" "Why, he went past just a little while ago, with the scribes and Pharisees and a great company."
"Where was he going?"
"Why, he was looking for Jesus, to betray Him."
"Why do you think that?"
"Because tonight at the feast Jesus said, 'One of you shall betray Me, and it is he to whom I give the morsel,' and after dipping it in the dish He handed it to Judas."
"Didn't you try to stop him in his dastardly work of betrayal?"
"No." "Well, don't you suppose Judas thought he would find Jesus here with you men?"
No, he never suspected that Jesus was near that bunch.
Judas knew that crowd.
He knew that first group out near the edge of the garden through and through.
Why do I think so?
I will tell you.

Jesus had gone up on the mount of transfiguration, taking with Him Peter, James and John, members of the second group, and while He was away a father whose boy was possessed by a devil came to the disciples who made up the first group, out near the edge of the garden, and begged them to cast the devil out of his boy.
Jesus had given His disciples power over unclean spirits, to drive them out, but instead of doing the work He gave them to do, they spent the time bickering over who would be greatest in the kingdom.
I wonder if there is a father in this world who has never had trouble with his boy.
This father was weighed down with trouble, all of it caused by the devil.
The devil is the cause of every saloon, every drunkard, every murder, every theft, every lie, every heartache, every house of shame.
All the deception, envy, malice, and filthy talk that come out of your mouth are prompted by the devil, and yet some people think I am throwing stones at them when I preach against the devil.
Some say, "Well, the devil pays, so let him stay.
We need the license money from the saloons to pave our streets and light our city."
Yes, and you need your saloons in order to keep your jails, penitentiaries, poorhouses and insane asylums filled.
Every saloon gives the devil that much better a chance to get your boy.
If you want the world to be better in time to come, keep the devil out of the boys and girls.
If you want to drive the devil out of the world, hit him with a cradle, not a crutch.
When Jesus returned from the mount, the sorrowing father ran to Him with his boy, crying, "If You are able to do anything, take pity on us and help us.
I brought my son to Your disciples, and they could not cast the devil out!"
That "if" implies a doubt.
The failure of those disciples to keep in touch with Jesus, so that they could have power to cast out devils, led the poor old father to doubt the power of Jesus.
The divine philosophy, as demonstrated by thousands of church members, breeds more infidels than all the Paines, Parkers and Ingersolls combined.
As a principle increases in its meaning, it decreases in the number of those who should adhere to that principle.
Suppose by education I mean everyone who can read and write; then there are about eighty-five million educated people in the United States.
But suppose that by education I mean everyone who has graduated from high school; then about one-fifth of the population would be classified as educated.
On the other hand, if by education I mean everyone who has graduated from a university or a college, one-half of one percent would come under that heading.
Suppose by your friends you mean all who shake your hand, smile and say, "How are you?
I am glad to see you."
You have scores of friends of that sort; but suppose by friends you mean all who will stand by you through thick and thin and defend you when they hear your name slandered—I fear they are sadly few.
Suppose by a Christian I mean everyone who has his name on a church roll; there are about twenty-six million in the United States, about equally divided between Catholics and Protestants.
On the other hand, suppose I mean every man and woman who is willing to do God's will; I question whether there are ten million who would die for Jesus.
I said to a minister one time, "How many members do you have?"
He said, "Eight hundred and seventy-two; but there are two hundred and seventy-eight I do not count."
I asked: "Of the number you do count, how many are helping in the meetings—singing in the choir, ushering, or doing personal work?"
Tears flowed down his cheeks as he said, "The largest number I have been able to muster on any one night was twenty-eight, and if my life depended on my making the number fifty, I would die!"
There we were, wearing out our lives trying to bring that God-forsaken, whisky-soaked, gambling-cursed, harlot-blighted town to her knees, and the church calmly looking on.
I sometimes doubt whether the church needs new members half as much as she needs the old bunch made over.

Judging by the way multitudes in the church live, you would think they imagined they had a through ticket to heaven in a Pullman palace car, and had left orders for the porter to wake them up when they pull into the yards of the New Jerusalem.
If that is the case, you are doomed to disappointment, for you will be sidetracked with a hot box.

If I had a hundred tongues, every tongue speaking a different language, in a different key, at the same time, I could not do justice to the splendid chaos that the world-loving, dancing, card-playing, whisky-guzzling, gin-fizzling, wine-sizzling, novel-reading crowd in the church brings to the cause of Christ.
There is only one voice from faithful preachers and workers about the church, and that is, "She is sick," but we say it in such painless, delicate terms that she seems to enjoy her invalidism.
About four out of five who have their names on our church rolls are doing nothing to bring the world to Christ, and the church is not one bit better for their presence.
To make amends for all this, Christians are making a great deal out of Lent.
I believe in a Lent that is kept three hundred and sixty-five days of the year.
I think it a travesty of the teachings of Christ that anyone can lay in such an overstock of piety in forty days that they can live like the devil the rest of the year.
That is an old trick of the devil.
The Jewish church struck that rock and was wrecked.
The Roman Catholic church struck it and was split.
The Protestant church is fast approaching the same doom.

One of the great dangers, as I see it, is assimilation to the world, the neglect of the poor, the substitution of forms for the facts of godliness, and a hireling ministry—which, all summed up, means a fashionable church with religion left out.
Formerly Methodists attended class meeting and gave testimony; now the class meeting has become a thing of the past.
Shouts of praise used to be heard.
Now such holy demonstrations are considered undignified.
Occasionally some godly old sister, who is a sort of connecting link between the old and the new, pipes up in a weak, negative, falsetto, apologetic kind of voice and says:
"Amen, Brother Sunday!"

I do not expect any of these ossified, petrified, mildewed, dyed-in-the-wool, stamped-on-the-cork, blown-in-the-bottle, horizontal, perpendicular Presbyterians or Episcopalians to shout "Amen!" but it would do you good to loosen up.
Many of you are hidebound.
I believe half of the professing Christians amount to nothing as a spiritual force.

They go to church and have a kindly regard for religion, but as for having a firm grip on God, a cheerful spirit of self-denial, enthusiastic service and prevailing prayer, and a willingness to strike hard, staggering blows against the devil, they are almost failures.
A shell has been invented which, when it strikes a ship, puts everyone on board to sleep.
Something of that kind seems to have hit our churches.
Jesus said to the members of the first group, near the edge of the garden, the largest in number, "Sit here."
To those who made up the second, He said, "My soul is sorrowful beyond measure, even to the point of death.
Wait here, and watch with Me.
Watch and pray, so that you do not enter into temptation.
The spirit truly is willing, but the flesh is weak."
But when He was alone He cried, "Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me; yet not My will, but Yours, be done."
Notice the progressive stages of revelation.
Not a word to Judas.
To the eight nearest the world, He said, "Sit here."
To Peter, James and John, He said, "Watch and pray."
When alone with the Father: "Your will be done."
He told the Father what He did not tell Peter, James and John.
He told them what He did not tell the group of eight, and what He did not tell Judas.
Do you wish God to reveal the deep things of the Spirit to you?
Then turn your back on sinful things and creep close to His side.
Jesus will never unfold His revelations to you when you are lined up in front of a bar drinking, or when you are at a baseball game on the Sabbath, or when you are living in sin.
Jesus did not ask the members of the first group, near the edge of the garden, to pray.
Perhaps they would have refused.
Every minister knows there are certain members of his church whom he never thinks of asking to lead in prayer.
In fact they never darken the door of a prayer meeting; if a card party takes place on prayer-meeting night, they are at the party.
Yet we wonder why this old sin-blighted world is not on her knees.
I am amazed that God is doing as well as He is, with the crowd He has to work with.
Please pardon a personal reference: I was born and raised, not in Old Kentucky, although my grandfather was born in Lexington, but in Old Iowa.
I was a rube of the rubes, a hayseed of the hayseeds.
I have greased my hair with goose grease.
I have blacked my boots with stove blacking.
I have wiped my face on a gunnysack towel.
I have eaten with my knife.
I have drunk coffee out of my saucer.
I have said "done it" when I should have said "did it," "came" when I should have said "come," and "seen" when I should have said "saw."
I am a graduate of the university of poverty and hard knocks, and I have taken postgraduate courses.
My autobiography could be summed up in one line from Gray's "Elegy": "The short and simple annals of the poor."
My father enlisted four months before I was born.
He went to the front with Company E, Twenty-third Iowa Infantry, but he never came back.
He died and was buried at Camp Patterson, Missouri.
I have battled my way since I was six years old.
I know all about the dark and seamy side of life.
If ever a man fought hard every inch of his way, I have.
One day Mother said, "Boys, I am going to send you to the Soldiers' Orphans' Home at Glenwood, Iowa."
We had to go to Ames to take the train.
We went to a little hotel to wait, and about one o'clock someone came and said, "Get ready for the train; it's coming."
I looked into Mother's face.
Her eyes were red; her hair was disheveled.
I said, "What's the matter, Mother?"
All the time Ed and I slept, Mother had been praying.
We went to the train.
Mother put one arm around me and the other around Ed, and sobbed as if her heart would break.
People walked by and looked at us, but they did not say a word.
Why? They did not know, and if they had, they would not have cared.
Mother knew; she knew that for years she would not see her boys.
We got on the train and cried, "Goodbye, Mother!" as the train pulled out.
We reached Council Bluffs.
It was cold, and we turned up our thin little coat collars around our necks and shivered.
We saw a hotel, and went up and asked a woman for something to eat.
She said, "What is your name?"
"My name is Willie Sunday, and this is my brother Ed," I said.
"Where are you going?"
"Going to the Soldiers' Orphans' Home at Glenwood."
She wiped away her tears and said, "My husband was a soldier, and he never came back.
He would not turn anyone away, and I certainly won't turn you boys away."
She threw her arms around us and said, "Come on in."
She gave us our breakfast, and our dinner too.
There was no train going out on the Burlington until afternoon.
We played around the rail yards.
We saw a freight train standing there, so we climbed into the caboose.
The conductor came along and said, "Where is your money?"
"Ain't got any." "Where are your tickets?"
"Ain't got any." "You can't ride without money or tickets.
I'll have to put you off."
We began to cry.
My brother handed him a letter of introduction to the superintendent of the Orphans' Home.
The conductor read it and handed it back as the tears rolled down his cheeks; then he said: "Just sit still, boys.
It won't cost you a cent to ride on my train."
It is only twenty miles from Council Bluffs to Glenwood, and as we rounded the curve the conductor said, "There is the Home on the hill."
Mother knew. Ed did not know.
I did not know. I went to sleep.
So did Ed; but Mother knew. She prayed.
Jesus knew. He prayed.
Peter, James and John went to sleep.
You cannot make me believe that if you knew, you would act as you do.
If you will tell me how much you read the Bible, how much you pray, and how much you do to help people to Jesus Christ, I will tell you what figure you point to on the spiritual thermometer.

The trouble is, you will be in church on Sunday morning, and will keep a little spot about eighteen inches square warm for half an hour, listen to the sermon, pick up a book and sing "Jesus Paid It All," when you have debts that are outlawed.
He does not pay them.
He does not pay for that hat, or that set of false teeth you are wearing.
You get up and say, "I am standing on the solid rock."
You are probably standing in a pair of shoes you have not paid for yet.
Let us get cleaned up for God, and see if the Lord will not do great things.
He will not send the wind to drive our ships unless we have the faith to lift our sails.
To the members of the first group Jesus said, "Sit here."
To those of the second group He said, "Watch and pray."
While His duty was to bear the sins of the world, there are multitudes in the church who do nothing.
They are mere ciphers.
At a funeral the preacher failed to appear.
The undertaker thought it would be a downright shame to lay the man away without something being said, and so decided to make a few remarks himself.
So when the time came he cleared his throat and in a pious whine said: "Dear friends, this corpse has been a member of this church for forty years!"
"Crucify Him!" cried the relentless rabble.
The clamor of that infuriated mob shook the temple from foundation to turret top.
Often in civil strife some such animosity and hatred of the multitudes had been witnessed.
Truly all the phantoms of hell seem to have assembled in Jerusalem, and out through the funeral gate poured the mob.
Here comes Judas, leading the devil's crowd.
Turning to the Pharisees, he said, "The one I kiss is He; hold Him fast."
See the smile on his hypocritical, sanctimonious face as he rushes forward shouting, "Hail, Master!" and kisses Him.
Jesus answers, "Judas, is it with a kiss that you betray the Son of Man?"
They seize Him and take Him to the High Priest's house, where He is condemned on false testimony to a felon's death on the cross.
